title: ITA Section 127(13): SR&ED Contract Payment Reductions
keyPhrase: ITA Section 127(13) SR&ED contract payment reductions
description: Avoid double-claiming R&D expenses in Canada. Learn how ITA Section 127(13) legislation enforces SR&ED contract payment reductions.
summary: For Canadian businesses claiming SR&ED, the Income Tax Act reduces contract payments for investment tax credit purposes: payments to arm's-length Canadian contractors and approved third parties are fully deductible in the section 37 pool, but only 80% qualify for the ITC. Payments to non-taxable suppliers are excluded, and non-arm's-length payers claim only through a Form T1146 transfer.

Payments to non-taxable suppliers are excluded, and non-arm's-length payers claim only through a Form T1146 transfer.
Executive Overview of the Canadian R&D Fiscal Architecture

Canada operates one of the most mature and financially significant research and development (R&D) fiscal incentive regimes in the industrialized world, anchored federally by the Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Tax Incentive Program. Administered jointly through the legislative policy oversight of the Department of Finance Canada and the operational, technical, and financial audit apparatus of the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA), the SR&ED Program represents the Government of Canada's single largest fiscal mechanism supporting business innovation. During the 2025–2026 fiscal cycle alone, the CRA allowed $4.6 billion in SR&ED investment tax credits across 23,677 processed claims, underscoring the centrality of statutory R&D credits to corporate capital allocation across the country.

The statutory architecture of the Canadian regime is codified within the federal Income Tax Act (R.S.C., 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.)) (the "Act" or "ITA") and the Income Tax Regulations (C.R.C., c. 945) (the "Regulations"). Unlike grant-based subsidies that rely on discretionary ministerial pre-approval or competitive budget pools, the federal SR&ED regime functions as a statutory entitlement. Any corporate, individual, trust, or partnership taxpayer that carries on qualifying scientific research or experimental development in Canada and satisfies the rigorous substantive and procedural requirements of the Act is legally entitled to two distinct, interlocking tax incentives. First, under the immediate and indefinite income deduction mechanism of subsection 37(1) of the Income Tax Act, taxpayers may pool allowable current and, for property acquired after December 15, 2024, capital SR&ED expenditures incurred in Canada to deduct against net income for tax purposes in the current taxation year, or carry the undeducted pool balance forward indefinitely to shelter taxable income in future taxation years. Second, under the investment tax credit provisions of subsections 127(5), 127(9), 127(10.1), and section 127.1 of the Income Tax Act, taxpayers earn an SR&ED Investment Tax Credit (ITC) calculated as a specified percentage—ranging from a 15% basic rate to a 35% enhanced rate—of their "SR&ED qualified expenditure pool". Depending on the taxpayer's corporate classification and expenditure profile, unused ITCs may be refunded directly in cash, applied to reduce Part I federal tax payable, carried back three taxation years, or carried forward up to twenty taxation years.

Between late 2024 and March 2026, the Canadian R&D tax landscape underwent its most profound structural transformation in over a decade. At the federal level, legislative reforms originating in the 2024 Fall Economic Statement and the 2025 Federal Budget were formally enacted through Bill C-15 (the Budget 2025 Implementation Act, No. 1, S.C. 2026, c. 3), which received Royal Assent on March 26, 2026. Retroactive to taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024 (that is, on or after December 16, 2024), Bill C-15 doubled the annual expenditure limit for the enhanced 35% refundable credit from $3,000,000 to $6,000,000, expanded the prior-year taxable capital phase-out band from the legacy $10,000,000–$50,000,000 range to $15,000,000–$75,000,000, extended eligibility for the 35% enhanced refundable credit to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs), and reinstated capital expenditures on depreciable property as qualified SR&ED expenditures. Concurrently, at the provincial level, Quebec enacted a sweeping overhaul for taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025, abolishing five legacy R&D tax credit programs and consolidating provincial support into the refundable Tax Credit for R&D and Pre-Commercialization (Crédit d'impôt pour la R-D et la précommercialisation — CRIC). This technical audit provides an exhaustive statutory, regulatory, judicial, and financial examination of the Canadian R&D tax regime as governed by current federal and provincial law.
Statutory Foundation and the Legal Definition of Qualifying R&D
Subsection 248(1) and the Three-Pillar Eligibility Framework

The threshold question in any Canadian R&D tax audit is whether the underlying technical activities satisfy the statutory definition of "scientific research and experimental development" set out in subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act. The statute defines SR&ED as a systematic investigation or search that is carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis. The statutory definition bifurcates qualifying activities into three primary scientific categories and one derivative category of directly commensurate support work. Basic research encompasses work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge without a specific practical application in view, whereas applied research encompasses work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge with a specific practical application in view. Experimental development—which in commercial practice accounts for the vast majority of corporate SR&ED claims in Canada—is defined as work undertaken for the purpose of achieving technological advancement for the purpose of creating new, or improving existing, materials, devices, products, or processes, including incremental improvements thereto. Complementing these three core branches is eligible support work, which covers work with respect to engineering, design, operations research, mathematical analysis, computer programming, data collection, testing, or psychological research, provided that such work is commensurate with the needs, and directly in support, of basic research, applied research, or experimental development that is undertaken in Canada by or on behalf of the taxpayer.

Conversely, subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act explicitly excludes several commercial and routine technical activities from the definition of SR&ED, even if they involve highly skilled personnel or complex technical execution. Excluded activities encompass market research or sales promotion; quality control or routine testing of materials, devices, products, or processes; research in the social sciences or the humanities; prospecting, exploring, or drilling for, or producing, minerals, petroleum, or natural gas; the commercial production of a new or improved material, device, or product or the commercial use of a new or improved process; style changes; and routine data collection. The legislative intent behind these exclusions is to ring-fence public tax expenditures so that fiscal subsidies target genuine scientific or technological risk rather than ordinary commercial product development or standard engineering customization.

To operationalize subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act, the CRA's Guidelines on the Eligibility of Work for Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Tax Incentives and Guide T4088 establish that an "SR&ED project" comprises a set of interrelated activities that collectively are necessary to resolve scientific or technological uncertainties in an attempt to achieve specific scientific or technological advancements, pursued through a systematic investigation or search in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis performed by qualified individuals. The CRA evaluates project eligibility at the level necessary to recognize all work required for the attempted advancement, distilling the statutory mandate into three mandatory pillars that are often framed administratively as two overarching requirements (the "Why" and the "How") and evaluated through five foundational questions.

The first pillar is scientific or technological uncertainty. A genuine technical problem, system constraint, or conflict must exist that cannot be resolved through standard practice, publicly available knowledge, routine engineering, or predictable application of known methodologies by a competent professional in the field. Crucially, technological uncertainty is distinct from commercial, financial, or project-management uncertainty; uncertainty as to whether a product can be built within a target cost budget or whether customers will adopt it does not qualify. Furthermore, the technological uncertainty must exist at the commencement of the investigation rather than being retroactively asserted after the fact at year-end.

The second pillar is scientific or technological advancement. The investigation must seek to generate new scientific knowledge or advance the underlying technology base—that is, an advancement in general technological understanding or capability in the field rather than merely expanding the internal technical proficiency of the claimant's own engineering staff. Significantly, commercial or technical success is not required under Canadian law. Failed or abandoned experiments fully qualify for SR&ED incentives provided they were undertaken to resolve a genuine technological uncertainty and generated technical knowledge demonstrating why a hypothesized solution cannot function under specific boundary conditions.

The third pillar is a systematic investigation or search. The claimant must address the technological uncertainty through a disciplined, structured methodology encompassing problem identification, the formulation of explicit technical hypotheses aimed at reducing or eliminating the uncertainty, the design and execution of planned experiments or rigorous mathematical and engineering analyses, the observation and documentation of empirical results, and logical conclusions or iterative hypothesis modifications based on those findings. Ad hoc trial-and-error tinkering conducted without an underlying causal hypothesis is systematically disallowed upon CRA technical review.
Judicial Interpretation and Tax Court of Canada Jurisprudence

The statutory language of subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act has been extensively interpreted by the Tax Court of Canada (TCC) and the Federal Court of Appeal (FCA), creating a binding body of jurisprudence that governs both CRA Research and Technology Advisors (RTAs) and taxpayers. The foundational judicial authority in Canadian SR&ED law is Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Ltd. v. The Queen, [1998] 3 C.T.C. 2520, 98 D.T.C. 1839 (TCC). In evaluating five hydraulic engineering projects involving physical scale modelling, Justice Donald Bowman articulated the canonical five-question test that remains the legal benchmark for judicial and administrative determinations of SR&ED eligibility across Canada.

Under Justice Bowman's framework in Northwest Hydraulic, the court must first ask whether there was a technological risk or uncertainty which could not be removed by routine engineering or standard procedures. Justice Bowman clarified that "routine engineering" describes techniques, procedures, and data that are generally accessible to competent professionals in the field; if a problem can be resolved by applying established engineering principles without fundamental uncertainty as to the outcome, it constitutes routine engineering and not SR&ED. Second, the court asks whether the person claiming to be doing SR&ED formulated hypotheses specifically aimed at reducing or eliminating that technological uncertainty. Third, the court examines whether the procedures adopted accorded with the total discipline of the scientific method, including the formulation, testing, and modification of hypotheses. Fourth, the court evaluates whether the process resulted in a technological advancement, meaning an advancement in general understanding. Fifth and finally, the court considers whether a detailed record of the hypotheses tested and results was kept as the work progressed.

Subsequent jurisprudence has substantially refined the application of the Northwest Hydraulic criteria across software engineering, industrial manufacturing, and shop-floor environments. In Zeuter Development Corporation v. The Queen, 2006 TCC 597, 2007 D.T.C. 41, [2006] T.C.J. No. 466 (QL), decided on October 31, 2006, Justice Little delivered a pivotal ruling governing software development claims. While Justice Little explicitly affirmed at paragraph 22 that software development can certainly be eligible as SR&ED, the Tax Court dismissed the taxpayer's appeal on the grounds that when uncertainties can be removed by competent software developers using standard programming practices and existing documentation, no qualifying technological uncertainty exists, and the appellant had failed to adduce evidence of systematic hypothesis testing. In contemporary CRA audit practice—particularly regarding artificial intelligence (AI), cloud-native Software-as-a-Service (SaaS) architectures, and enterprise software—the CRA relies heavily on Zeuter Development to disallow routine software customization, standard debugging, writing integrations with external Application Programming Interfaces (APIs) using vendor-supplied documentation, and prompt engineering against commercial foundation models, which the CRA treats as optimization of a known tool rather than investigation under technological uncertainty. Conversely, developing novel multi-tenant concurrency architectures, custom real-time collaboration engines, custom authorization and access-control systems, or novel algorithmic optimizations under strict computational scale constraints qualifies where existing methods cannot predict system behaviour.

Further doctrinal clarity emerged in Joel Theatrical Rigging Contractors (1980) Ltd. v. The Queen, 2017 TCC 6, decided by Justice Sommerfeldt. This ruling provides critical legal precedent on three recurring audit disputes. First, at paragraph 17, Justice Sommerfeldt acknowledged that there is no definitive statutory definition of the term "routine engineering," requiring a contextual factual assessment of the state of standard procedure in the relevant industry. Second, at paragraph 26, after reviewing the jurisprudence considering the meaning of the word "hypothesis," Justice Sommerfeldt concluded that a hypothesis is simply a statement to be tested by an experiment or a trial, dispelling the notion that shop-floor or industrial claimants must frame their hypotheses in academic prose. Third, and most importantly for audit defence, at paragraph 33 Justice Sommerfeldt summarized the characteristics demonstrating that a scientific method was adopted, and at paragraph 46 noted that while keeping progressive records is part of the five-question analysis, a written contemporaneous record of hypotheses tested and results kept is not an absolute legal prerequisite if the taxpayer can establish through other credible evidence that systematic testing in fact occurred.

The practical impact of Joel Theatrical Rigging is illustrated in shop-floor and industrial manufacturing decisions such as Les Abeilles Service de Conditionnement Inc. v. The Queen (TCC) and Manning Canning Kitchens Inc. v. His Majesty the King (2025 TCC). In Manning Canning Kitchens Inc., the appellant encountered severe thermal processing failures resulting in exploding cans during product development. The Minister of National Revenue denied the claim, asserting that Manning Canning had not undertaken a systematic investigation or search in developing its product. Applying Justice Sommerfeldt's analytical framework from paragraphs 17, 26, 33, and 46 of Joel Theatrical Rigging, Justice Bodie found that the appellant had established a genuine technological uncertainty, formulated and tested hypotheses through a systematic investigation, maintained sufficient records of the hypotheses tested and results obtained as its work progressed, and achieved a technological advancement that solved the exploding-can problem. Consequently, the Tax Court ruled that the appellant had discharged its burden on all five questions and held that the project qualified as SR&ED.

body.text: Federal Legislative Reforms and Rate Architecture Under Bill C-15
Enactment of Bill C-15 and Expansion of the Expenditure Limit

The financial value of a Canadian SR&ED claim is governed by section 127 and section 127.1 of the Income Tax Act. Historically, the enhanced 35% refundable SR&ED Investment Tax Credit was restricted exclusively to qualifying Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations (CCPCs), as defined in subsection 125(7) of the Income Tax Act, up to an annual expenditure limit of $3,000,000, which phased out when the corporation's (and its associated group's) prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada ranged between $10,000,000 and $50,000,000.

Following policy proposals introduced in the 2024 Fall Economic Statement and confirmed in the 2025 Federal Budget, Parliament enacted Bill C-15, which received Royal Assent on March 26, 2026. The statutory amendments in Bill C-15 apply to taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024 (that is, on or after December 16, 2024) and fundamentally recalibrate the expenditure limit and corporate eligibility rules. Under amended subsection 127(10.2) of the Income Tax Act, the maximum annual expenditure limit on which a qualifying corporation can earn the enhanced 35% ITC under subsection 127(10.1) has been doubled from $3,000,000 to $6,000,000, surpassing the $4,500,000 cap initially announced in earlier economic proposals. Consequently, the maximum annual refundable federal ITC available at the 35% enhanced rate has doubled from $1,050,000 to $2,100,000 per year.

Simultaneously, for CCPCs determining their expenditure limit under the standard taxable capital method, Bill C-15 expanded the phase-out thresholds for prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada, aggregated across the CCPC and all associated corporations. The lower phase-out threshold at which the expenditure limit begins to taper increased from $10,000,000 to $15,000,000, and the upper phase-out cap at which the expenditure limit reaches nil increased from $50,000,000 to $75,000,000. For taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, a CCPC's annual expenditure limit is determined by the statutory formula in subsection 127(10.2) of the Income Tax Act:

In this statutory formula, variable A is nil ($0) if the combined taxable capital employed in Canada of the corporation and all associated corporations for the immediately preceding taxation year is $15,000,000 or less, leaving the full $6,000,000 expenditure limit untouched. Where prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada exceeds $15,000,000, variable A is equal to the lesser of $60,000,000 and the excess of prior-year taxable capital over $15,000,000:
A = lesser of $60,000,000 and (Prior-Year Taxable Capital Employed in Canada − $15,000,000)

Accordingly, for every $10 of prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada above $15,000,000, the $6,000,000 expenditure limit is reduced by $1 (a 10% linear taper across the $60,000,000 phase-out band), reaching nil at $75,000,000. A critical point of statutory verification for auditors and tax planners is that taxable income does not enter this formula or reduce the federal SR&ED expenditure limit. Subsection 127(10.2) of the Income Tax Act was amended in 2019 to permanently remove prior-year taxable income as a factor in determining a corporation's expenditure limit. Any legacy guidance that describes a taxable income reduction does not reflect current federal law.

Strict statutory rules govern associated corporate groups and short fiscal periods. Under subsections 127(10.21) to 127(10.4) of the Income Tax Act, associated CCPCs must share a single $6,000,000 expenditure limit. Specifically, subsection 127(10.21) deems the expenditure limit of an associated CCPC to be nil unless the associated group files an allocation agreement in prescribed form—Schedule 49 (T2SCH49)—under subsection 127(10.3) assigning the shared limit among group members. If the associated group fails to file an agreement within 30 days after notice in writing by the Minister of National Revenue, the Minister allocates the expenditure limit among the corporations under subsection 127(10.4). Furthermore, where an associated CCPC has more than one taxation year ending in the same calendar year and is associated in two or more of those taxation years with another CCPC having a taxation year ending in that same calendar year, specific proration and alignment rules under subsection 127(10.5) apply, alongside anti-avoidance provisions for deemed non-association under subsections 127(10.22) and 127(10.23) and refundable credit sharing rules under subsections 127.1(2.2) and 127.1(2.3). Independently of association, under paragraph 127(10.5)(b) of the Income Tax Act, where a Canadian-controlled private corporation has a short taxation year of less than 51 weeks, its otherwise determined expenditure limit is prorated by multiplying the limit by the number of days in the taxation year divided by 365:
Prorated Expenditure Limit = Expenditure Limit × (Number of Days in the Taxation Year ÷ 365)
Inclusion of Eligible Canadian Public Corporations and the Revenue Election

One of the most consequential policy shifts enacted in Bill C-15 is the elimination of the "public listing penalty" that previously stripped Canadian innovation companies of the 35% refundable SR&ED rate the moment they completed an Initial Public Offering (IPO) or reverse takeover. For taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs)—as defined in subsection 127(9) of the Income Tax Act—are eligible to earn the enhanced 35% ITC rate on up to $6,000,000 of qualified SR&ED expenditures on the same statutory footing as CCPCs.

Because public corporations frequently carry substantial balance-sheet equity raised in public capital markets, applying a taxable capital phase-out to public entities would prematurely disqualify pre-profit public R&D companies, such as clinical-stage biotechnology or capital-intensive hardware firms. Consequently, Parliament established a distinct revenue-based phase-out mechanism for ECPCs and introduced an elective parallel regime for CCPCs. Under subsections 127(10.6) and 127(10.61) of the Income Tax Act, for an ECPC—or an ECPC that is a member of a consolidated corporate group, referencing the definition of "Consolidated Financial Statements" in subsection 233.8(1) of the Income Tax Act—the gradual reduction of the $6,000,000 expenditure limit is calculated using the average annual revenue of the last three fiscal years rather than prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada. Consolidated ECPC groups must similarly file an expenditure limit allocation agreement under subsection 127(10.62), failing which the Minister allocates the limit under subsection 127(10.63) if no agreement is filed within 30 days after notice in writing.

Crucially, Bill C-15 also enacted subsections 127(10.31) and 127(10.32) of the Income Tax Act, which permit a CCPC (under subsection 127(10.31) where it is not associated with another corporation throughout the year, and under subsection 127(10.32) where it has associated corporations) to formally elect on the prescribed form to have its $6,000,000 expenditure limit gradual reduction determined the same way an ECPC's is—on a three-year average of annual revenue instead of prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada. This statutory election creates a major second-order tax-planning opportunity for asset-heavy but low-revenue private Canadian companies—such as clean-technology, semiconductor, biomanufacturing, or deep-tech enterprises—whose debt and equity financing pushes their prior-year taxable capital above $15,000,000 (or even above $75,000,000) while their three-year average commercial revenue remains low enough to preserve the full $6,000,000 enhanced expenditure limit.
Investment Tax Credit Rates, Refundability Matrix, and Carryover Mechanics

The rate at which qualified SR&ED expenditures generate federal ITCs under subsections 127(5) and 127(9) of the Income Tax Act, and the extent to which those credits are convertible into immediate cash refunds under section 127.1 (including subsections 127.1(1) and 127.1(2.01)), depend on four intersecting variables: the taxpayer's legal classification, whether the expenditures fall within or exceed the $6,000,000 expenditure limit, whether the expenditures are of a current nature (including the Prescribed Proxy Amount) or a capital nature, and whether the taxpayer owes Part I federal income tax.

The enhanced ITC rate of 35% is available to qualifying CCPCs and, for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, ECPCs on qualified SR&ED expenditures up to their available annual expenditure limit (maximum $6,000,000) pursuant to subsection 127(10.1) of the Income Tax Act. The basic ITC rate of 15% applies to all qualified SR&ED expenditures incurred by non-qualifying corporations (such as foreign-controlled subsidiaries and large public corporations exceeding the ECPC revenue threshold), individuals, and trusts, as well as to qualified expenditures incurred by CCPCs and ECPCs in excess of their annual expenditure limit.

Refundability under section 127.1 of the Income Tax Act exhibits important structural nuances between CCPCs and ECPCs. For a qualifying CCPC, 100% of the unclaimed balance of the ITC earned at the 35% enhanced rate on qualified current expenditures and its Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) is refundable in cash, while 40% of the unclaimed balance of the ITC earned at the 35% enhanced rate on qualified capital expenditures is refundable in cash. On qualified expenditures exceeding the CCPC's expenditure limit—which earn the 15% basic ITC rate—a qualifying CCPC receives a 40% cash refund of the unclaimed 15% ITC (representing an effective 6% cash refund on excess expenditures), with the remaining 60% of the credit non-refundable. For an Eligible Canadian Public Corporation (ECPC) in taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, the refundability within the $6,000,000 expenditure limit mirrors that of a CCPC: 100% of the unclaimed balance of the 35% enhanced ITC on current expenditures and the PPA is refundable, and 40% of the unclaimed balance of the 35% enhanced ITC on capital expenditures is refundable. However, on expenditures exceeding the $6,000,000 expenditure limit, an ECPC's 15% basic ITC is strictly non-refundable (0% cash refund), whereas a qualifying CCPC retains 40% refundability on that excess band. For non-resident-controlled corporations and other non-qualifying corporations, the 15% basic ITC is entirely non-refundable and can only reduce Part I tax payable. Furthermore, no amount is considered an ITC in respect of an SR&ED expenditure made in the course of earning income if any of the claimant's income is exempt from Part I tax. Partnerships do not claim ITCs directly because a partnership is not a corporation; rather, the partnership's SR&ED expenditures and ITC allocations flow through to its partners to be claimed on their respective returns under subsection 127(8) of the Income Tax Act, subject to limited-partner at-risk restrictions under paragraph 127(8.2)(a).

Any non-refundable ITC—or any refundable ITC that a taxpayer elects not to receive as a cash refund—is first applied to reduce Part I federal tax payable for the current taxation year under subsection 127(5) of the Income Tax Act. Unused SR&ED ITCs may be carried back 3 taxation years or carried forward up to 20 taxation years to offset Part I tax payable in those periods. Concurrently, undeducted SR&ED expenditures in the subsection 37(1) expenditure pool may be carried forward indefinitely to reduce net income for tax purposes in future taxation years.

body.text: Qualifying Expenditures, Overhead Elections, and Capital Cost Restoration
Direct Labour, Specified Employee Caps, and Unpaid Remuneration

Across virtually all Canadian industries, salary or wages—as defined in subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act—of employees directly engaged in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada constitute the primary component of qualified SR&ED expenditures. Under the CRA SR&ED Salary or Wages Policy and Guide T4088, eligible labour encompasses the gross salary or wages of technical personnel (scientists, engineers, software developers, technicians, and directly engaged technical supervisors) apportioned strictly to the time spent performing hands-on experimental development, scientific research, or eligible support work in Canada (reported on Line 300 for non-specified employees and Line 305 for specified employees of Form T661), plus the employer's share of payroll levies. Under limited statutory conditions (reported on Lines 307 and 309 of Form T661), permissible salary or wages for SR&ED work performed outside Canada may also be claimed.

However, the Income Tax Act and Income Tax Regulations enforce stringent anti-avoidance restrictions on the remuneration of "specified employees" to prevent closely held corporations from disguising dividend distributions or profit-sharing as refundable R&D wages. Under subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act, a "specified employee" is an employee who does not deal at arm's length with the employer or who is a "specified shareholder" of the employer—generally an individual who owns, directly or indirectly at any time in the year, 10% or more of the issued shares of any class of the corporation or a related corporation. When a founder, executive, or principal engineer is a specified employee, three statutory constraints govern their remuneration.

First, subsection 37(9) of the Income Tax Act (and Guide T4088, Line 305) excludes any remuneration based on profits or any bonus paid to a specified employee from SR&ED expenditures. The CRA defines a bonus as an amount paid in addition to the employee's normal pay. While a bonus remains deductible to the corporation as an ordinary business expense, it earns zero SR&ED credit for a specified employee. Furthermore, taxable benefits under section 6 of the Income Tax Act and employee stock option benefits under section 7 are excluded from SR&ED salary and from the proxy salary base for all employees, whether specified or not, alongside bonuses and profit-based pay under Regulation 2900(9).

Second, under subsection 37(9.1) of the Income Tax Act, the maximum direct SR&ED salary or wages that may be claimed for a single specified employee is capped at 5 times the Year's Maximum Pensionable Earnings (YMPE) determined for purposes of the Canada Pension Plan for the calendar year in which the taxation year ends, prorated by the number of days in the taxation year that the individual was a specified employee:
Maximum Direct SR&ED Salary = 5 × YMPE × (Days in the Taxation Year as a Specified Employee ÷ 365)

For the 2026 taxation year, the YMPE established by the Government of Canada is $74,600.00. Consequently, the maximum direct SR&ED salary or wages claimable for one specified employee in 2026 is $373,000 (5 × $74,600), compared to $218,500 (5 × $43,700) in 2007. Where a specified employee is employed by two or more associated corporations, this ceiling must be allocated among the associated corporations using Form T1174.

Third, where the claimant elects to use the Proxy Method to compute overhead, subsection 2900(7) of the Income Tax Regulations imposes a second, lower ceiling on the amount of a specified employee's salary that can enter the proxy "salary base" (calculated on Lines 850 to 860 in Part 5, Section A of Form T661). Specifically, the proxy salary base inclusion for a specified employee is restricted to the lesser of 75% of the specified employee's total salary or wages for the year (combining both SR&ED and non-SR&ED duties, but excluding bonuses, remuneration based on profits, taxable benefits, and prior-year unpaid wages paid in the year) or 2.5 times the YMPE for the calendar year in which the taxation year ends, prorated by the number of days in the taxation year that the claimant employed the individual (with no proration for the time during the year that the employee was not a specified employee):
Proxy Salary Base Inclusion = lesser of (75% × Total Salary or Wages) and (2.5 × YMPE × Days Employed in the Taxation Year ÷ 365)

For the 2026 taxation year (YMPE = $74,600), the 2.5 × YMPE proxy salary base cap is $186,500. This creates a critical planning dynamic for startup founders who devote nearly all of their working time to hands-on R&D. For example, if a founder-shareholder earns a salary of $100,000 and devotes 70% of their time to SR&ED, their direct SR&ED salary is $70,000 and their proxy salary base is also $70,000—since $70,000 is below both 75% of total salary ($75,000) and the $186,500 cap—generating a 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount of $38,500, total qualified spending of $108,500, and a 35% refundable credit of $37,975. However, if that same founder spent 90% of their time on SR&ED, $90,000 would qualify as direct SR&ED salary, but the proxy salary base would be capped at $75,000 (75% of $100,000) under Regulation 2900(7).

Strict statutory timing rules also govern unpaid remuneration and unpaid current expenditures. Under subsection 78(4) of the Income Tax Act, any salary or wages incurred in a taxation year that remain unpaid on the day that is 180 days after the end of the taxation year are deemed not to have been incurred in that year (subtracted on Line 315 of Form T661), and are instead treated as incurred only in the subsequent taxation year in which they are actually paid (added on Line 310 of Form T661), both for the section 37 deduction and the section 127 credit. Crucially, under Regulation 2900(9) and the CRA Prescribed Proxy Amount Policy, a prior-year unpaid salary amount that is paid late can enter direct SR&ED salary in the year it is paid, but it never enters the proxy salary base, resulting in the permanent forfeiture of the 55% overhead proxy on late-paid wages. Similarly, under subsection 127(26) of the Income Tax Act, unpaid non-wage current SR&ED expenditures (such as contractor or material invoices) remaining unpaid 180 days after the end of the taxation year are excluded from qualified expenditures for ITC purposes in the year incurred (Line 520 of Form T661) and are added back only in the subsequent taxation year in which they are paid (Line 500 of Form T661).
Traditional Method Versus Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) Election

To account for R&D overhead, a taxpayer must elect on Page 1, Part 1 of Form T661 (fields 160 or 162) between two mutually exclusive calculation methods for each taxation year: the Proxy Method (under subsection 37(10) of the Income Tax Act and section 2900 of the Income Tax Regulations) or the Traditional Method (under subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(A) of the Income Tax Act). The claimant must make this choice when first filing Form T661 for the taxation year, and the election is irrevocable for that year (if the claimant is a partnership, the election is valid only if made on behalf of all members by an authorized partner).

Under the Proxy Method, the claimant does not specifically identify, track, or allocate overhead and other indirect expenditures for SR&ED. Instead, the claimant computes a notional amount—the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA)—equal to 55% of the salary base (reported on Line 820 in Part 5, Section B of Form T661) pursuant to subsection 2900(4) of the Income Tax Regulations. While the PPA rate was 65% in 2012 and prior years and 60% in 2013, it has been fixed at 55% since 2014. The salary base (Line 818) is calculated using only the eligible salaries and wages of employees directly engaged in SR&ED in Canada (Lines 810 to 814 for non-specified employees, plus the capped amounts on Lines 850 to 860 for specified employees, including rules for all-or-substantially-all [ASA] employees under Regulation 2900(5)). The proxy salary base never includes contractor costs, third-party payments, or materials. In addition, the PPA is subject to an overall cap in Part 5, Section B based on non-SR&ED business expenses (calibrated at $55 CAD per $100 of eligible salary) so that the notional proxy cannot exceed the enterprise's total actual overhead.

The tax mechanics of the PPA require careful distinction between section 37 and section 127 of the Income Tax Act. Under paragraph 127(9)(b) of the Income Tax Act, the PPA is explicitly defined as a "qualified expenditure" (entered on Line 502 of Form T661) and earns the full SR&ED ITC, including the 100% refundable 35% enhanced rate for CCPCs and ECPCs. However, the PPA is relevant only for the purposes of calculating SR&ED ITCs; it is a notional figure and is never added to the subsection 37(1) pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures. The actual overhead expenditures that the PPA represents—such as office supplies, general-purpose office equipment, heat, water, electricity, telephones, salaries or wages for support staff not directly engaged in SR&ED, travel, training, property taxes, and maintenance and upkeep of SR&ED premises, facilities, or equipment—remain deductible as ordinary business expenses under section 9 and paragraph 18(1)(a) of the Income Tax Act, rather than under paragraph 37(1)(a).

Conversely, under the Traditional Method, the claimant enters "0" for the PPA and must specifically identify, track, and allocate overhead and other expenditures that are directly related and incremental to the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada—meaning eligible expenditures directly attributable to SR&ED that would not have been incurred had the SR&ED not been carried out. These substantiated overhead costs are claimed on Line 360 of Form T661, included in the subsection 37(1) pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures, and included in qualified expenditures to earn SR&ED ITCs. While the Proxy Method is overwhelmingly favoured by software, AI, and engineering firms whose qualifying costs are dominated by researcher salaries because it eliminates the administrative burden of tracking overhead, the Traditional Method remains valuable for heavy industrial or laboratory operations where actual incremental overhead exceeds 55% of direct SR&ED labour.
Materials Consumed, Materials Transformed, Cloud Infrastructure, and Recapture

Under both the Traditional Method (subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(A) of the Income Tax Act) and the Proxy Method (subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(V)), a claimant may separately claim 100% of the cost of materials consumed or materials transformed in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada, whether purchased from Canadian or foreign suppliers, provided the materials are used directly in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada. Since February 23, 1998, the statutory framework and the CRA Materials for SR&ED Policy have distinguished between materials consumed and materials transformed based on whether the physical or digital inputs retain value after the experimental work concludes.

Materials are classified as "consumed" in the prosecution of SR&ED when they are destroyed or rendered virtually valueless as a result of the SR&ED—for example, galvanized metal parts subjected to destructive testing, or wood, chemicals, seeds, growth media, and agar destroyed during laboratory experimentation. However, the mere fact that an item is used while SR&ED is performed does not make it "materials consumed". The CRA Materials for SR&ED Policy explicitly excludes broken or used lab supplies (such as petri dishes, beakers, flasks, and pipettes), cleaning supplies, general utilities (such as water, electricity, oil, natural gas, or propane—unless a claimant clearly identifies, meters, and documents with a reasonable, verifiable allocation method a specific portion of water or energy directly consumed as a material in the SR&ED process), CDs/DVDs, and used lubricants such as engine oil. Under the Proxy Method, such general supplies and utilities are subsumed within the 55% PPA.

For software, data analytics, artificial intelligence, and SaaS companies, cloud computing and data processing costs—specifically Amazon Web Services (AWS), Google Cloud Platform (GCP), and Microsoft Azure compute instances—used directly for SR&ED experimentation, staging, and testing environments are eligible 100% as materials consumed in the prosecution of SR&ED. However, CRA Financial Reviewers strictly enforce the accounting boundary between R&D cloud environments and commercial production cloud infrastructure. Cloud hosting charges and third-party API costs incurred to serve live commercial customers constitute Cost of Goods Sold (COGS) / Cost of Revenue and are ineligible for SR&ED. To substantiate cloud computing claims as materials consumed, claimants must segment cloud bills by environment, apply resource tags in AWS, GCP, or Azure to separate "development/staging/R&D" workloads from "production" workloads, and maintain separate general ledger accounts.

When materials, components, or supplies are incorporated into a prototype, custom product, commercial asset, experimental production run, or commercial production with experimental development that is not destroyed or rendered valueless, they are classified as "materials transformed" in the prosecution of SR&ED. While 100% of the cost of materials transformed is deductible under section 37 and earns SR&ED ITCs in the year of transformation, subsections 127(27) to 127(36) of the Income Tax Act and the CRA Recapture of Investment Tax Credit Policy enforce mandatory ITC recapture if the property (or another property that incorporates the property) is subsequently sold or converted to commercial use.

Under subsection 127(27) of the Income Tax Act, when a property on which an SR&ED ITC was claimed—including materials transformed, all-or-substantially-all (ASA) equipment, shared-use equipment (SUE), animals and other growing things used in SR&ED, or property acquired through an SR&ED contract—is disposed of or converted to commercial use, the taxpayer must add back to its Part I tax payable for that year an amount equal to the lesser of the original ITC earned on the property and the amount calculated by applying the original ITC percentage rate to the proceeds of disposition (as defined in subsection 13(21) of the Income Tax Act, if sold at arm's length) or the fair market value of the property (if converted to commercial use or sold to a non-arm's length party). Crucially, under Section 5.1 of the CRA Recapture of Investment Tax Credit Policy, for recapture purposes the "cost" of a property cannot exceed the amount paid by the claimant to acquire the property from another person; it does not include any amount paid by the claimant to maintain, modify, or transform the property, nor does it include internal SR&ED salaries, wages, or overhead costs imputed to the property. Nor are the proceeds of disposition allocated between material costs and SR&ED salaries. For example, if a claimant incurs $300,000 in SR&ED expenditures ($135,000 in materials transformed and $165,000 in internal SR&ED salaries) and claims a 35% ITC of $105,000, and subsequently sells the resulting asset, the maximum recapture under subsection 127(27) is capped at 35% of the $135,000 material cost ($47,250), leaving the ITC earned on internal salaries untouched. Specific recapture rules also govern allocating taxpayers (subsection 127(29)), partnerships (subsection 127(30)), and non-arm's length dispositions (subsection 127(34)).
Subcontractors, Third-Party Payments, and Restored Capital Expenditures

Beyond internal employees and materials, Canadian enterprises frequently engage external contractors, research institutes, and equipment suppliers. Under subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i.01) of the Income Tax Act, payments made to an arm's-length contractor to perform eligible SR&ED work in Canada on the claimant's behalf (reported on Line 340 of Form T661) are 100% deductible in the subsection 37(1) expenditure pool. However, under paragraph 127(9)(a)(ii) of the Income Tax Act, only 80% of an eligible arm's-length contract expenditure qualifies for SR&ED ITCs, with the mandatory 20% reduction subtracted on Line 529 of Form T661. Only the technical SR&ED work portion of a subcontract qualifies; project management, commercial design, and non-technical tasks must be excluded. Moreover, the contractor must be a "taxable supplier" in Canada; current expenditures for an SR&ED contract paid or payable to a person or partnership that is not a taxable supplier in respect of the expenditure (such as a foreign subcontractor not subject to Canadian tax) are excluded from the ITC base on Line 528 of Form T661. Where SR&ED is subcontracted to a non-arm's length party, the payer cannot claim ITCs directly on the contract payment, but the non-arm's length parties may file a joint agreement on Form T1146 to transfer the performer's qualified SR&ED expenditures to the payer (reported on Schedule C and Line 508 of Form T661).

Similarly, under subparagraphs 37(1)(a)(ii) and (iii) and paragraph 127(9)(a)(ii) of the Income Tax Act, third-party payments made to approved universities, colleges, research institutes, or non-profit R&D consortia (reported on Line 370 of Form T661 and substantiated via Schedule A and Form T1263) are 100% deductible under subsection 37(1) and 80% eligible for SR&ED ITCs (with the 20% adjustment on Line 529).

A landmark feature of Bill C-15 is the restoration of capital expenditures to the SR&ED program. Capital expenditures had been removed from SR&ED eligibility in 2014. Effective for depreciable property acquired after December 15, 2024 (that is, on or after December 16, 2024), capital expenditures for machinery, equipment, prototyping tools, testing apparatus, and laboratory instruments—as well as qualifying lease costs—are once again eligible for the section 37 deduction and are included as qualified expenditures for the section 127 ITC. To qualify, the depreciable property must be new to the claimant's business, used in Canada, and intended to be used all or substantially all (90% or more of its operating time) for SR&ED in Canada. As noted in the rate matrix, for CCPCs and ECPCs within their $6,000,000 expenditure limit, the 35% enhanced ITC earned on qualified capital expenditures is 40% refundable in cash. (Under legacy and ongoing lease rules in Form T661, lease costs of equipment used less than 90% of the time for SR&ED are excluded under the Proxy Method, whereas historical shared-use equipment [SUE] rules deemed 1/4 of the capital cost eligible per period with 25% first-term and 50% second-term conversion recapture rates under section 127).

For capital assets that do not satisfy the strict 90% SR&ED use threshold—such as servers, switches, and network infrastructure shared between commercial operations and R&D—taxpayers deduct capital costs through Capital Cost Allowance (CCA) under paragraph 20(1)(a) of the Income Tax Act once the property becomes "available for use" under subsection 13(26) (as opposed to paragraph 18(1)(b), which denies capital outlays as current deductions under paragraph 18(1)(a), and section 67, which requires all expenses to be reasonable in amount). Under Regulation 1100 of the Income Tax Regulations and Bill C-15, properties in Class 44 (patents), Class 46 (data network infrastructure equipment, which carries a normal 30% CCA rate; note that Class 52 is closed to new additions), and Class 50 (general-purpose electronic data processing equipment and systems software, such as servers, which carries a normal 55% CCA rate) acquired after April 15, 2024, and available for use before 2027 qualify for 100% immediate expensing in the first year, with the standard half-year rule in Regulation 1100(2) suspended. Furthermore, for broader depreciable property acquired after 2024 and available for use before 2030, Regulation 1100(2) provides a reinstated accelerated investment incentive equal to 3 times the normal first-year CCA deduction (or 1.5 times where the half-year rule would not normally apply), stepping down to 2 times (or 1.25 times) for property available for use from 2030 to 2033, before returning to normal rates after 2033.

body.text: Administrative Governance, Prescribed Forms, and Compliance Procedures
Institutional Roles of the CRA, Department of Finance, and NRC IRAP

The governance of Canada's R&D incentive ecosystem is divided among three federal institutions whose mandates intersect during the lifecycle of an R&D project. The Department of Finance Canada holds statutory responsibility for tax policy design and legislative drafting under the Income Tax Act and Income Tax Regulations. The Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) administers the SR&ED Program and adjudicates all claims through two specialized audit functions: Research and Technology Advisors (RTAs), who review the scientific and technological eligibility of claimed projects and verify whether claimed expenditures are commensurate with the technical work, and Financial Reviewers, who audit general ledger reconciliations, payroll records, specified employee calculations, contract terms, and overhead elections. Alongside the tax system, the National Research Council of Canada Industrial Research Assistance Program (NRC IRAP) provides direct innovation grants and technical advisory support to Canadian small and medium-sized enterprises. Because amounts received under IRAP for SR&ED-type work constitute government assistance under subsection 127(9) of the Income Tax Act, claimants must report all IRAP funding in Part 1 and on Line 515 of Form T661, reducing the qualified SR&ED expenditure pool under subsection 127(18) (while any repayments of government and non-government assistance that previously reduced the deductible SR&ED expenditure pool are added back on Schedule B / Line 445 of Form T661).
Architecture of Form T661, Schedule 31, and Supplementary Schedules

To access the subsection 37(1) deduction and the subsection 127(5) investment tax credit, the CRA Filing Requirements Policy, subsection 37(11), and paragraph 127(9)(m) of the Income Tax Act mandate that a claimant submit prescribed forms containing prescribed information. The centrepiece of every claim is Form T661 (Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Expenditures Claim), interpreted via CRA Guide T4088. Form T661 is structured into distinct parts that must be completed with precision. Part 1 captures general corporate information, the total number of projects claimed, IRAP assistance disclosures, and the irrevocable election between the Proxy Method and Traditional Method in fields 160 or 162, together with the signed Certification and Election. Part 2 (Section B) contains the project-by-project technical narratives, which are subject to strict word limits and must be written in clear, concise technical language by personnel familiar with the scientific or technical content to establish how each project met the technological uncertainty, systematic investigation, and technological advancement requirements.

Part 3 of Form T661 calculates allowable SR&ED expenditures (Lines 300 to 390) and determines the subsection 37(1) pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures available for deduction in the year (Line 455 / Line 460) and the pool balance carried forward to future years (Line 470). Part 4 calculates the qualified SR&ED expenditures for ITC purposes (Lines 500 to 570), incorporating additions for prior-year unpaid non-wage amounts paid in the year under subsection 127(26) (Line 500), the Prescribed Proxy Amount (Line 502), and qualified expenditures transferred via Form T1146 (Line 508), while subtracting provincial government assistance (Lines 513 to 517), other government assistance (Line 515), current expenditures unpaid 180 days after year-end under subsection 127(26) (Line 520), non-taxable supplier contracts (Line 528), the 20% reduction on arm's-length contracts and third-party payments (Line 529), and prescribed expenditures not allowed by regulations (Line 530). Part 5 (Sections A and B) computes the salary base (Lines 810 to 860) and the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount (Line 820) for claimants electing the Proxy Method. Part 6 requires claimants to record and allocate expenditures on a project-by-project basis across all claimed SR&ED projects. Finally, Part 9 mandates complete disclosure of claim preparer information (including contingency fee arrangements, which in the Canadian market typically range from 15% to 25% of the approved credit, or flat-fee/retainer structures) to mitigate civil penalty exposure.

Crucially, Form T661 calculates the expenditure pools but does not compute the investment tax credit itself. To earn and claim the ITC, corporations must file a completed Schedule T2SCH31 (Investment Tax Credit – Corporations) with their T2 Corporation Income Tax Return, whereas individuals must file Form T2038(IND) (Investment Tax Credit (Individuals)). Depending on the claimant's transactions, Form T661 must be supplemented by Form T1145 (Agreement to Allocate Assistance for SR&ED Between Persons Not Dealing at Arm's Length), Form T1146 (Agreement to Transfer Qualified Expenditures Incurred in Respect of SR&ED Contracts Between Persons Not Dealing at Arm's Length), Form T1174 (Agreement Between Associated Corporations to Allocate Salary or Wages of Specified Employees for SR&ED), and Form T1263 (Third-Party Payments for SR&ED), alongside Schedule T2SCH49 for associated CCPC expenditure limit allocations. Under subsection 150.1(2.1) of the Income Tax Act, corporations must file their T2 returns and schedules electronically via Corporation Internet Filing using CRA-certified software (with a signed Form T183CORP where an EFILE-certified preparer transmits on the corporation's behalf), as paper filing triggers a $1,000 penalty under subsection 162(7.2). Under paragraph 230(4)(b) of the Income Tax Act, all supporting accounting and technical records must be retained for six years from the end of the last taxation year to which they relate.
The 18-Month Statutory Filing Bar and Audit Defence Protocols

The most critical procedural requirement in Canadian R&D tax compliance is the statutory reporting deadline governed by subsection 37(11) and paragraph 127(9)(m) of the Income Tax Act. Under paragraph 127(9)(m), no amount may be included in a taxpayer's investment tax credit if the taxpayer does not file with the Minister a prescribed form containing prescribed information in respect of the amount on or before the day that is one year (12 months) after the taxpayer's filing-due date for the particular taxation year. Similarly, if the claimant has not identified an expenditure on the prescribed form by that 12-month post-filing-due-date deadline, the expenditure is legally excluded from SR&ED expenditures under section 37.

Because a corporation's T2 income tax return filing-due date is 6 months after its taxation year-end (whereas its corporate balance of tax is due 2 months after year-end under paragraph 157(1)(b) of the Income Tax Act), the SR&ED reporting deadline for a corporation is exactly 18 months after the end of the taxation year in which the expenditures were incurred. For example, a corporation with a December 31, 2024 fiscal year-end faces a firm SR&ED filing deadline of June 30, 2026. These filing requirements apply equally to any original or amended prescribed form for SR&ED; if a claimant forgets to claim an expenditure or project, an amended Form T661 and Schedule 31 must be submitted within that same 18-month window. Miss the 18-month deadline and the claim is permanently barred: there is no late-filing relief for SR&ED.

Once filed, the CRA typically processes straightforward SR&ED refunds within 60 to 120 days, whereas first-time claims or complex submissions selected for technical and financial review require 120 to 180 days. When a claim is selected for review, a CRA Research and Technology Advisor (RTA) frequently requests a technical interview with the claimant's Chief Technology Officer or lead engineers and inspects supporting project records. The primary cause of audit disallowance is the lack of contemporaneous documentation proving that hypotheses and experiments were recorded as the work progressed rather than reconstructed at year-end. Robust audit defence requires integrating SR&ED tracking directly into daily engineering workflows: maintaining Git commit histories, sprint logs, architecture decision records, laboratory test results, prototype failure logs, monthly developer timesheets coded to specific SR&ED projects, purchase orders, subcontractor agreements, and tagged cloud infrastructure reports.

body.text: Provincial R&D Tax Regimes and Federal-Provincial Stacking Mechanics
Government Assistance Stacking and Pool Reduction Mathematics

Provincial and territorial governments across Canada offer supplementary R&D tax credits that stack onto the federal SR&ED credit. However, calculating the net combined return requires applying the statutory "government assistance" reduction rules under subsections 127(9) and 127(18) of the Income Tax Act. Because provincial R&D tax credits constitute government assistance, they must be deducted on Lines 513 to 517 of Form T661 from the federal SR&ED qualified expenditure pool before the federal 35% or 15% ITC rate is calculated. Simply adding headline provincial and federal percentages together overstates the combined benefit. Instead, the net combined credit rate (R) on a qualifying expenditure base subject to a provincial credit rate (rp) and a federal ITC rate (rf) is expressed as:
R = r<sub>p</sub> + r<sub>f</sub> × (1 − r<sub>p</sub>)

To illustrate this interaction with a calculation for a British Columbia-based CCPC incurring $1,000,000 in qualifying R&D expenditures within its $6,000,000 expenditure limit, the corporation first earns a 10% refundable BC SR&ED tax credit of $100,000. That $100,000 provincial credit reduces the federal qualified expenditure base from $1,000,000 to $900,000. Applying the 35% federal enhanced rate to the net $900,000 federal expenditure base produces a $315,000 federal refund (0.35 × $900,000), resulting in a combined federal and provincial cash recovery of $415,000 (41.5% net effective rate). Similarly, a tech startup in Ontario spending $300,000 on qualifying developer salaries and subcontractors receives $24,000 in 8% refundable Ontario OITC alongside its federal SR&ED credit.
Ontario R&D Tax Credit Ecosystem (OITC, ORDTC, and OBRITC)

Ontario administers three distinct corporate R&D tax credits that harmonize with the federal SR&ED definition and are claimed directly on schedules attached to the T2 Corporation Income Tax Return. First, the Ontario Innovation Tax Credit (OITC), claimed on Schedule 566 (and entered on line 468 of Schedule 5), provides an 8% refundable tax credit to qualifying CCPCs with a permanent establishment in Ontario on up to $3,000,000 of annual qualified Ontario SR&ED expenditures (a maximum annual refundable credit of $240,000). The $3,000,000 OITC expenditure limit phases out when the corporation's (or associated group's) prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada lies between $25,000,000 and $50,000,000. Claimants must file Schedule 566 alongside federal Form T661 within 18 months of the end of the taxation year.

Second, the Ontario Research and Development Tax Credit (ORDTC), claimed on Schedule 508, provides a 3.5% non-refundable tax credit on eligible Ontario SR&ED expenditures to all corporations with an Ontario permanent establishment, regardless of size or foreign ownership. Unused ORDTC credits may be carried back 3 taxation years or carried forward 20 taxation years to offset Ontario corporate income tax payable. When a CCPC claims both the OITC on Schedule 566 and the ORDTC on Schedule 508, the OITC reduces the eligible expenditure pool for the ORDTC, and specific adjustments apply where the federal PPA interacts with government assistance calculations on Schedule 508.

Third, the Ontario Business-Research Institute Tax Credit (OBRITC), claimed on Schedules 568 and 569, provides a 20% refundable tax credit on qualified contract expenditures incurred under an eligible R&D contract with an approved Ontario research institute (such as an eligible Ontario university, college, or hospital research institute). Beyond SR&ED, Ontario software and multimedia enterprises may also qualify for the Ontario Interactive Digital Media Tax Credit (OIDMTC), which provides a 40% refundable credit (including up to $100,000 of marketing and distribution expenses) or a 35% refundable credit on eligible Ontario labour and contractor costs directly attributable to developing interactive multimedia products.
Quebec's 2025–2026 CRIC Consolidation and Abolition of Legacy Credits

In Quebec, corporate tax incentives are administered independently by Revenu Québec via the CO-17 corporate income tax return. Effective for taxation years (and partnership fiscal periods) beginning after March 25, 2025, the Government of Quebec enacted a landmark reform that eliminated five legacy R&D tax credits and consolidated provincial support into a single, modernized measure: the Tax Credit for R&D and Pre-Commercialization (Crédit d'impôt pour la R-D et la précommercialisation — CRIC). Specifically, for fiscal periods beginning after March 25, 2025, Quebec abolished the former Tax Credit for Salaries and Wages (R&D) (previously claimed on Form RD-1029.7), the Tax Credit for University Research or Research Carried Out by a Public Research Centre or a Research Consortium, the Tax Credit for Private Partnership Pre-Competitive Research, the Tax Credit for Fees and Dues Paid to a Research Consortium, and the Tax Credit for Technological Adaptation Services. Concurrently, because product design conducted as a continuation of R&D in Quebec now qualifies as a pre-commercialization activity under the CRIC, Quebec adjusted the in-house and outside-consultant design tax credits so that industrial design expenditures no longer qualify under those legacy design credits.

The CRIC is claimed by filing Revenu Québec Form RD-1029.8.CR-T (supported by Form RD-1029.8.EN-T for associated group expenditure limit agreements and Form RD-1029.8.PR-T for pre-commercialization disclosures) with the CO-17 return, or no later than 12 months after the CO-17 filing-due date. Unlike the legacy regime, the CRIC covers three broad pillars of innovation work carried out in Quebec: traditional R&D activities, pre-commercialization activities performed as a continuation of R&D activities (such as testing, prototyping, industrial product design, and technological validation), and eligible capital expenditures for the acquisition of new depreciable property (excluding land, buildings, or rights in a building) used in Quebec almost exclusively in eligible R&D or pre-commercialization activities, considered incurred when the property becomes available for use. Eligible expenditure categories encompass salaries and wages of employees engaged in eligible activities (including directly related support roles), consideration paid to subcontractors performing eligible work in Quebec, payments to certain research organizations, and eligible capital property acquisitions.

The CRIC calculation replaces the former $83,333 salary cap and legacy asset-based threshold with a unified Exclusion Threshold equal to the greater of $50,000 (adjusted for the number of days in the taxation year) or an amount calculated using the Quebec basic personal amount applicable to the employees involved. Once a corporation's net eligible expenditures exceed this Exclusion Threshold, the CRIC provides a 100% refundable tax credit at an enhanced rate of 30% on the first $1,000,000 of eligible expenditures above the threshold, and a base refundable rate of 20% on all eligible expenditures exceeding that $1,000,000 band. If a corporation claims the CRIC as a member of a qualified partnership, its percentage interest is applied to the partnership's eligible expenditures, but the 30% enhanced rate does not apply, restricting partnership claims to the 20% base rate.
British Columbia, Alberta, and Other Provincial Regimes

In western Canada, British Columbia provides a 10% BC SR&ED tax credit on eligible BC R&D expenditures, which is 100% refundable for qualifying CCPCs and non-refundable for other corporations. In Alberta, the Innovation Employment Grant (IEG) provides a refundable grant/credit on eligible Alberta R&D expenditures up to an annual cap, structured around a prior-year baseline and a taxable-capital phase-out that is statutorily tied to subsection 127(10.2) of the federal Income Tax Act.

body.text: Strategic Conclusions and Technical Compliance Recommendations

The legislative enactment of Bill C-15 on March 26, 2026, combined with Quebec's transition to the CRIC regime for taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025, fundamentally alters the strategic calculus for corporate R&D tax planning in Canada. To capture the full benefit of these statutory reforms while insulating claims from CRA technical and financial audit adjustments, corporate tax leaders and technical executives should immediately execute several integrated governance measures.

First, mid-market CCPCs and Canadian public corporations must re-model their expenditure limit entitlements for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024. With the federal expenditure limit doubled to $6,000,000 (yielding up to $2,100,000 in annual 35% refundable credits) and the taxable capital phase-out band raised to $15,000,000–$75,000,000 under subsection 127(10.2) of the Income Tax Act, private companies previously phased out of the enhanced tier can once again access refundable credits. Furthermore, capital-intensive CCPCs whose balance-sheet debt and equity exceed $15,000,000 in taxable capital should model the new election under subsections 127(10.31) and 127(10.32) to calculate their expenditure limit taper using the three-year average annual revenue method, while qualifying public companies should verify their status as Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) under subsection 127(9).

Second, closely held corporations employing technical founders or 10%+ shareholders ("specified employees") must structure executive compensation as regular base salary rather than bonuses or profit-based pay, which are barred from SR&ED eligibility under subsection 37(9) of the Income Tax Act. Tax directors must track the 2026 YMPE ($74,600.00) caps—which limit a specified employee's direct SR&ED salary to $373,000 (5 × $74,600) under subsection 37(9.1) and their proxy salary base to the lesser of 75% of total salary or $186,500 (2.5 × $74,600) under Regulation 2900(7)—and ensure all accrued salaries and contractor invoices are paid within 180 days of fiscal year-end under subsections 78(4) and 127(26) so that the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount is never forfeited under Regulation 2900(9).

Third, hardware, manufacturing, and clean-tech enterprises acquiring new machinery, testing rigs, or laboratory equipment after December 15, 2024, must implement asset registers and usage logs proving ≥90% (all or substantially all) SR&ED usage in Canada to claim the restored section 37 deduction and section 127 ITC, while utilizing 100% immediate first-year CCA expensing under Classes 44, 46, and 50 (for property acquired after April 15, 2024, and available for use before 2027) under Regulation 1100 and Bill C-15 for shared-use digital infrastructure. Concurrently, software and AI claimants must enforce strict AWS, GCP, and Azure resource tagging to segregate eligible R&D compute ("materials consumed") from commercial production hosting (COGS).

Finally, enterprises operating in Quebec must overhaul their internal project accounting for taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025, transitioning from abolished Form RD-1029.7 wage claims to Form RD-1029.8.CR-T to capture the 30% and 20% refundable CRIC rates across both R&D and downstream pre-commercialization validation, design, and prototyping activities. Above all, corporate tax departments must institutionalize real-time contemporaneous technical documentation aligned with the five-question Northwest Hydraulic and Joel Theatrical Rigging standards and enforce internal filing calendars well ahead of the unextendable 18-month statutory reporting bar under subsection 37(11) and paragraph 127(9)(m) of the Income Tax Act.
